claim: RAW macrophages typically formed a chalice-shaped phagocytic cup and completed phagocytosis in approximately 3 minutes when engulfing DAAMPs.
source: RAW macrophages typically formed a chalice-shaped phagocytic cup and completed phagocytosis in a similar timeframe (~3 min) as previously reported for much stiffer (2–3 GPa) polystyrene particles (Horsthemke et al., 2017; Figure 1a, Video 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by direct observation from LLSM imaging data presented in Figure 1a and Video 1, with quantification shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Target constriction defined by discrete spots of deformation appeared around the circumference of the DAAMP at the rim of the phagocytic cup.
source: We observed target constriction defined by discrete spots of deformation that appeared around the circumference of the DAAMP at the rim of the phagocytic cup (Figure 1d, Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by direct visualization in Figure 1d and Video 2 showing deformations on the target surface.

claim: Indentations traveled parallel to the direction of phagocytic cup elongation along the length of the DAAMP particle until cup closure.
source: Interestingly, these indentations traveled parallel to the direction of phagocytic cup elongation, along the length of the DAAM particle until cup closure and were associated with ~400 nm maximum target constriction for 1.4 kPa DAAMPs (Video 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Video 2 and quantified in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Maximum target constriction for 1.4 kPa DAAMPs was approximately 400 nm.
source: Interestingly, these indentations traveled parallel to the direction of phagocytic cup elongation, along the length of the DAAM particle until cup closure and were associated with ~400 nm maximum target constriction for 1.4 kPa DAAMPs (Video 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) exhibited similar mechanical progression during phagocytosis as RAW macrophages, albeit with smaller deformations.
source: To determine whether this behavior was also present in primary macrophages, we also imaged bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) transfected with mEmerald-Lifeact and observed a similar mechanical progression, albeit with smaller deformations (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by LLSM imaging data of BMDMs shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Bulk compressive stresses during phagocytic cup progression were approximately 0.5 kPa.
source: In addition to local deformations in RAW macrophages, we also observed bulk compressive stresses during phagocytic cup progression (~0.5 kPa) and after complete internalization of the DAAMPs (up to 1.5 kPa), leading to a dramatic reduction in DAAMP diameter (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of target volume changes shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Bulk compressive stresses after complete internalization of DAAMPs reached up to 1.5 kPa.
source: In addition to local deformations in RAW macrophages, we also observed bulk compressive stresses during phagocytic cup progression (~0.5 kPa) and after complete internalization of the DAAMPs (up to 1.5 kPa), leading to a dramatic reduction in DAAMP diameter (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of target volume changes shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Compressive forces observed up to 400 Pa at sites of target constriction are substantially greater than previously reported stresses of approximately 100 Pa using softer 0.3 kPa targets.
source: Force analysis (see Materials and methods) revealed compressive stresses up to 400 Pa at these sites (Figure 2c), which is substantially greater than our previous findings of stresses of ~100 Pa using softer targets with Young's modulus 0.3 kPa (Vorselen et al., 2020b), and suggests that force exertion during phagocytosis may be regulated based on target rigidity.
evidence: The claim is supported by force calculations from MP-TFM data shown in Figure 2c and comparison to previous work cited.

claim: Force exertion during phagocytosis may be regulated based on target rigidity.
source: Force analysis (see Materials and methods) revealed compressive stresses up to 400 Pa at these sites (Figure 2c), which is substantially greater than our previous findings of stresses of ~100 Pa using softer targets with Young's modulus 0.3 kPa (Vorselen et al., 2020b), and suggests that force exertion during phagocytosis may be regulated based on target rigidity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that compressive stresses increase with target stiffness, comparing 0.3 kPa and 1.4 kPa targets.

claim: Total compressive forces in the phagocytic rim increased from approximately 1 nN in early-stage phagocytosis (fraction engulfed ~22%) to approximately 10 nN in later stages (fraction engulfed >50%).
source: The total compressive forces in the phagocytic rim, which lead to target constriction, increased from ~1 nN in early-stage phagocytosis (fraction engulfed ~22%) to ~10 nN in later stages (fraction engulfed >50%).
evidence: The claim is supported by force analysis data shown in Figure 2j.

claim: Shear forces were approximately 7-fold lower than observed normal forces, independent of the stage of phagocytic engulfment.
source: The shear forces were consistent in magnitude with reported values using TFM during frustrated phagocytosis on planar gels of similar rigidity (Rougerie and Cox, 2020) and were ~7-fold lower than the observed normal forces, independent of the stage of phagocytic engulfment (Figure 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative comparison of normal and shear stresses shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Normal forces dominate the mechanical interaction in phagocytosis, which is in stark contrast with lamellipodial extensions during cell migration where shear forces dominate.
source: This suggests that normal forces dominate the mechanical interaction in phagocytosis, which is in stark contrast with lamellipodial extensions during cell migration where shear forces dominate (Case and Waterman, 2015; Legant et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data showing normal forces are 7-fold higher than shear forces (Figure 2d) and comparison to cited literature on cell migration.

claim: F-actin accumulation near the front of the phagocytic cup was approximately 5-fold higher than at the cup base.
source: This analysis confirmed a clear accumulation of F-actin near the front of the phagocytic cup (~5-fold higher than at the cup base), which precisely colocalized with the site of maximal applied inward normal forces regardless of engulfment stage, as illustrated by quantifying the surface mean curvature (Figure 2f).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of F-actin intensity profiles shown in Figure 2f.

claim: F-actin accumulation precisely colocalized with the site of maximal applied inward normal forces regardless of engulfment stage.
source: This analysis confirmed a clear accumulation of F-actin near the front of the phagocytic cup (~5-fold higher than at the cup base), which precisely colocalized with the site of maximal applied inward normal forces regardless of engulfment stage, as illustrated by quantifying the surface mean curvature (Figure 2f).
evidence: The claim is supported by spatial correlation analysis shown in Figure 2f.

claim: An apparent contractile ring was observed in almost all (~96%) phagocytic cups.
source: Direct analysis of target constriction and F-actin peak intensity for each phagocytic cup (Figure 2i, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) revealed an apparent contractile ring in almost all (~96%) cups.
evidence: The claim is supported by systematic analysis of all phagocytic cups shown in Figure 2i and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The location of the actin contractile ring along the phagocytic axis correlated extremely well with phagocytic progression (ρ = 0.93, p = 3.2 × 10–29).
source: The location of this actin contractile ring along the phagocytic axis correlated extremely well with phagocytic progression (ρ = 0.93, p = 3.2 × 10–29) and led to target constriction increasing from ~80 nm in early-stage (fraction engulfed <40%) to ~210 nm in late-stage cups (fraction engulfed >70%).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical correlation analysis shown in Figure 2i.

claim: Target constriction increased from approximately 80 nm in early-stage phagocytosis (fraction engulfed <40%) to approximately 210 nm in late-stage cups (fraction engulfed >70%).
source: The location of this actin contractile ring along the phagocytic axis correlated extremely well with phagocytic progression (ρ = 0.93, p = 3.2 × 10–29) and led to target constriction increasing from ~80 nm in early-stage (fraction engulfed <40%) to ~210 nm in late-stage cups (fraction engulfed >70%).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of target constriction at different stages shown in Figure 2i.

claim: In early stages of phagocytosis, net pulling (or outward normal) forces were observed throughout the phagocytic cup and particularly at the base (~3 nN total force, > 100 Pa tensile stresses).
source: Strikingly, in early stages of phagocytosis, net pulling (or outward normal) forces were observed throughout the phagocytic cup and particularly at the base (~3 nN total force, > 100 Pa tensile stresses) (Figure 2j), whereas in late-stage phagocytosis strong net compressive stresses were observed.
evidence: The claim is supported by force analysis data shown in Figure 2j.

claim: In late-stage phagocytosis strong net compressive stresses were observed.
source: Strikingly, in early stages of phagocytosis, net pulling (or outward normal) forces were observed throughout the phagocytic cup and particularly at the base (~3 nN total force, > 100 Pa tensile stresses) (Figure 2j), whereas in late-stage phagocytosis strong net compressive stresses were observed.
evidence: The claim is supported by force analysis data shown in Figure 2j.

claim: Target constriction was diminished upon inhibition of the Arp2/3 complex and myosin-II activity.
source: Target deformation analysis and force calculations revealed that target constriction was diminished upon inhibition of the Arp2/3 complex and myosin-II activity, while formin inhibition had a relatively modest effect (Figure 3c,d, Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analysis of target deformations under different drug treatments shown in Figure 3c,d.

claim: Formin inhibition had a relatively modest effect on target constriction.
source: Target deformation analysis and force calculations revealed that target constriction was diminished upon inhibition of the Arp2/3 complex and myosin-II activity, while formin inhibition had a relatively modest effect (Figure 3c,d, Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analysis of target deformations under SMIFH2 treatment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: The loss of target constriction coincided with a strong reduction (~40%) in F-actin accumulation at the rim of the cup.
source: The loss of target constriction coincided with a strong reduction (~40%) in F-actin accumulation at the rim of the cup, as well as a 50% broadening of the typical narrow (~2 μm) F-actin band observed in the DMSO control (Figure 3d,e, Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of F-actin intensity shown in Figure 3d,e.

claim: There was a 50% broadening of the typical narrow (~2 μm) F-actin band upon Arp2/3 or myosin-II inhibition.
source: The loss of target constriction coincided with a strong reduction (~40%) in F-actin accumulation at the rim of the cup, as well as a 50% broadening of the typical narrow (~2 μm) F-actin band observed in the DMSO control (Figure 3d,e, Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of F-actin band width shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Upon myosin-II inhibition alone, the loss of F-actin at the rim of the cup was complemented by a small, but significant (p = 0.04), increase in F-actin density at the base of the cup.
source: Of note, upon myosin-II inhibition alone, the loss of F-actin at the rim of the cup was complemented by a small, but significant (p = 0.04), increase in F-actin density at the base of the cup (Figure 3d,f, Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of F-actin intensity at the cup base shown in Figure 3f.

claim: Myosin-II may be promoting actin disassembly at the base of the phagocytic cup during internalization, similar to the role of myosin-II in disassembling the F-actin network at the cell rear during cell motility.
source: This observation suggests that myosin-II may be promoting actin disassembly at the base of the phagocytic cup during internalization, similar to the role of myosin-II in disassembling the F-actin network at the cell rear during cell motility (Wilson et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of increased F-actin at the cup base upon myosin-II inhibition and comparison to cited literature on cell motility.

claim: Inhibition of the Arp2/3 complex strongly reduced phagocytosis after 15 min and uptake remained low after longer incubation.
source: Similar to previous reports using large polystyrene particles (Rotty et al., 2017), inhibition of the Arp2/3 complex strongly reduced phagocytosis after 15 min and uptake remained low after longer incubation (Figure 3g, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by phagocytic efficiency assays shown in Figure 3g and Figure 3—figure supplement 2, and comparison to cited literature.

claim: Uptake was not significantly affected by Blebbistatin treatment.
source: Meanwhile, uptake was not significantly affected by Blebbistatin treatment and slightly reduced upon SMIFH2 treatment (Figure 3g, Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by phagocytic efficiency assays shown in Figure 3g.

claim: Uptake was slightly reduced upon SMIFH2 treatment.
source: Meanwhile, uptake was not significantly affected by Blebbistatin treatment and slightly reduced upon SMIFH2 treatment (Figure 3g, Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by phagocytic efficiency assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: A significant change in the observed distribution of cup stages was found upon myosin-II inhibition, but not Arp2/3 or formin perturbation, compared to DMSO-treated control cells.
source: Our analysis revealed a significant change in the observed distribution of cup stages upon myosin-II inhibition, but not Arp2/3 or formin perturbation, compared to DMSO-treated control cells (Figure 3h and Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of cup stage distributions shown in Figure 3h.

claim: In Blebbistatin-treated cells, there was an >6-fold enrichment of cups that were beyond 90% engulfment, but not yet closed (p = 1.9 × 10–4).
source: Specifically, in the Blebbistatin-treated cells, we found an >6-fold enrichment of cups that were beyond 90% engulfment, but not yet closed (p = 1.9 × 10–4).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of late-stage cup frequency shown in Figure 3h.

claim: The high prevalence of late-stage phagocytic cups upon myosin-II inhibition suggests a specific role for myosin-II in cup closure.
source: This high prevalence of late-stage phagocytic cups suggests a specific role for myosin-II in cup closure.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of accumulated late-stage cups upon Blebbistatin treatment.

claim: General particle deformations, as measured by the decrease in target sphericity, were strongly reduced upon both CK666 and Blebbistatin treatment throughout phagocytosis.
source: Throughout phagocytosis, general particle deformations, as measured by the decrease in target sphericity, were strongly reduced upon both CK666 and Blebbistatin treatment (Figure 3i).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of target sphericity shown in Figure 3i.

claim: Overall target deformations were reduced in all stages of phagocytosis upon Arp2/3 inhibition.
source: Whereas overall target deformations were reduced in all stages of phagocytosis upon Arp2/3 inhibition, myosin-II inhibition only significantly affected phagocytic force generation at later stages, after 50% engulfment (Figure 3i).
evidence: The claim is supported by stage-specific analysis of target deformations shown in Figure 3i.

claim: Myosin-II inhibition only significantly affected phagocytic force generation at later stages, after 50% engulfment.
source: Whereas overall target deformations were reduced in all stages of phagocytosis upon Arp2/3 inhibition, myosin-II inhibition only significantly affected phagocytic force generation at later stages, after 50% engulfment (Figure 3i).
evidence: The claim is supported by stage-specific analysis of target deformations shown in Figure 3i.

claim: There is a specific role for myosin-II in late-stage phagocytosis despite previous data that shows myosin-II is dispensable for phagocytosis.
source: This analysis strongly suggests that there is a specific role for myosin-II in late-stage phagocytosis despite previous data that shows myosin-II is dispensable for phagocytosis (Figure 3g; Jaumouillé et al., 2019; Olazabal et al., 2002; Rotty et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the stage-specific effects of myosin-II inhibition and comparison to cited literature.

claim: Branched actin assembly plays an important role throughout phagocytic progression.
source: The strong effect of Arp2/3 inhibition on phagocytic efficiency and target deformations throughout phagocytosis, and the lack of effect on the distribution of cups-in-progress, suggests that branched actin assembly plays an important role throughout phagocytic progression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the consistent effects of CK666 treatment across all stages of phagocytosis.

claim: Actin-rich puncta appeared as oblong or triangular tooth-like projections locally indenting the target surface along the internal rim of the phagocytic cup.
source: Indeed, we frequently observed actin-rich puncta that appeared as oblong or triangular tooth-like projections locally indenting the target surface along the internal rim of the phagocytic cup (Figure 4a) and sometimes deeper within the cup (Figure 4b).
evidence: The claim is supported by direct visualization in Figure 4a and 4b.

claim: Similar actin 'teeth' were formed by primary murine BMDMs, bone marrow-derived dendritic cells (BMDCs), and HL-60 human neutrophils when challenged with IgG-functionalized DAAMPs.
source: Similar actin 'teeth' were formed by primary murine BMDMs, bone marrow-derived dendritic cells (BMDCs), and HL-60 human neutrophils when challenged with IgG-functionalized DAAMPs, suggesting that these structures are a common feature of phagocytosis (Figure 4c).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data from multiple cell types shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Actin teeth are a common feature of phagocytosis across different phagocytic cell types.
source: Similar actin 'teeth' were formed by primary murine BMDMs, bone marrow-derived dendritic cells (BMDCs), and HL-60 human neutrophils when challenged with IgG-functionalized DAAMPs, suggesting that these structures are a common feature of phagocytosis (Figure 4c).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of teeth in multiple cell types.

claim: Cells treated with the Arp2/3 inhibitor CK666 exhibited an 80% reduction in the number of actin teeth per cup compared to control cells.
source: Cells treated with the Arp2/3 inhibitor CK666, and to a lesser extent cells treated with the formin inhibitor SMIFH2, exhibited a reduction in the number of actin teeth per cup (80% and 40% reduction, respectively) compared to control cells treated with DMSO (Figure 4d, Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of tooth number shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Cells treated with the formin inhibitor SMIFH2 exhibited a 40% reduction in the number of actin teeth per cup compared to control cells.
source: Cells treated with the Arp2/3 inhibitor CK666, and to a lesser extent cells treated with the formin inhibitor SMIFH2, exhibited a reduction in the number of actin teeth per cup (80% and 40% reduction, respectively) compared to control cells treated with DMSO (Figure 4d, Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of tooth number shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: Target-deforming phagocytic teeth include both Arp2/3- and formin-nucleated actin filaments, similar to podosomes.
source: This result suggests that, like podosomes (van den Dries et al., 2019b), target-deforming phagocytic teeth include both Arp2/3- and formin-nucleated actin filaments.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the effects of both CK666 and SMIFH2 on tooth number and comparison to cited literature on podosomes.

claim: A strong decrease (~50%) in the number of actin teeth was observed upon myosin-II inhibition.
source: Surprisingly, a strong decrease (~50%) in the number of actin teeth was also observed upon myosin-II inhibition.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of tooth number shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Tooth size and depth were reduced upon CK666 or Blebbistatin treatment, but the effect size was small (<15%).
source: Although tooth size and depth were reduced upon CK666 or Blebbistatin treatment, the effect size was small (<15%), suggesting that 'teeth' are resilient structures that, once formed, have well-defined properties (Figure 4d).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of tooth size and depth shown in Figure 4d.

claim: 'Teeth' are resilient structures that, once formed, have well-defined properties.
source: Although tooth size and depth were reduced upon CK666 or Blebbistatin treatment, the effect size was small (<15%), suggesting that 'teeth' are resilient structures that, once formed, have well-defined properties (Figure 4d).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that tooth properties are only modestly affected by drug treatments.

claim: Teeth moved forward with a speed of approximately 5.6 μm/min, similar to previously reported values for podosome-like structures on very stiff substrates during frustrated phagocytosis.
source: More commonly, however, teeth moved forward with a speed of ~5.6 μm/min, similar to the previously reported values for podosome-like structures on very stiff substrates during frustrated phagocytosis (Ostrowski et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by tracking data from LLSM shown in Figure 4e and comparison to cited literature.

claim: Teeth within the same phagocytic cup appeared to move in a coordinated fashion, with similar speed and direction, and even with observed collective speed changes.
source: Strikingly, teeth within the same phagocytic cup appeared to move in a coordinated fashion, with similar speed and direction, and even with observed collective speed changes (Figure 4e, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by tracking data from LLSM shown in Figure 4e and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Phagocytic teeth, like podosomes, are mechanically interlinked at the mesoscale.
source: This suggests that phagocytic teeth, like podosomes (Meddens et al., 2016; Proag et al., 2015), are mechanically interlinked at the mesoscale.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the coordinated movement of teeth and comparison to cited literature on podosomes.

claim: RAW macrophages assembled actin teeth more frequently when fed softer targets.
source: However, by assessing actin distribution, RAW macrophages assembled actin teeth more frequently when fed softer targets (Figure 4i).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analysis of tooth frequency on 1.4 kPa vs 6.5 kPa targets shown in Figure 4i.

claim: Phagocytic teeth may play a role in the overall mechanosensitivity of phagocytosis.
source: This is consistent with our findings that there is less overall F-actin accumulation in the cup rim on stiffer targets (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and suggests that phagocytic teeth may play a role in the overall mechanosensitivity of phagocytosis (Beningo and Wang, 2002; Jaumouillé et al., 2019; Sosale et al., 2015; Vorselen et al., 2020b; Vorselen et al., 2020a).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the mechanosensitive formation of teeth and comparison to cited literature on phagocytic mechanosensitivity.

claim: Approximately 70% of teeth were positioned at the rim of the cup.
source: We first distinguished the teeth positioned at the rim of the cup (~70% of teeth), which likely contribute to target constriction, from those deeper in the cup, based on their distance from the cup rim (Figure 4f, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by spatial analysis of tooth positions shown in Figure 4f.

claim: The number of teeth per cup and tooth size correlated with overall constriction in DMSO-treated cells and between groups treated with actomyosin activity inhibitors.
source: Indeed, the number of teeth per cup and tooth size correlated with overall constriction in DMSO-treated cells and between groups treated with actomyosin activity inhibitors CK666, SMIFH2, and Blebbistatin (Figure 4g, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4g and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Teeth numbers increased only slightly with phagocytic progression.
source: Teeth numbers increased only slightly with phagocytic progression, which suggests that they are formed quickly early on in phagocytosis and are then typically maintained at constant numbers throughout engulfment (Figure 4h).
evidence: The claim is supported by stage-specific analysis of tooth number shown in Figure 4h.

claim: Teeth are formed quickly early on in phagocytosis and are then typically maintained at constant numbers throughout engulfment.
source: Teeth numbers increased only slightly with phagocytic progression, which suggests that they are formed quickly early on in phagocytosis and are then typically maintained at constant numbers throughout engulfment (Figure 4h).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that tooth numbers remain relatively constant across phagocytic stages.

claim: Teeth size and depth increased significantly but modestly during phagocytic progression.
source: Teeth size and depth increased significantly but modestly during phagocytic progression (Figure 4h, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by stage-specific analysis of tooth properties shown in Figure 4h and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Teeth activity is insufficient to explain the greater degree of target constriction in late-stage phagocytosis.
source: Remarkably, this revealed that teeth activity is indeed sufficient to account for total target constriction in early-stage phagocytosis (<50% engulfment), but insufficient to explain the greater degree of target constriction later in the process (Figure 4j).
evidence: The claim is supported by elasticity theory simulations shown in Figure 4j.

claim: Additional myosin-II-based contractile forces are present in late-stage phagocytosis.
source: This is consistent with additional myosin-II-based contractile forces in late-stage phagocytosis, as suggested by our observations using Blebbistatin.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the discrepancy between simulated and observed constriction in late-stage phagocytosis and the effects of Blebbistatin treatment.

claim: The Arp2/3 complex and its activator, WASP, colocalized with the actin teeth.
source: Consistent with our earlier results showing a decrease in the number of teeth after treating cells with the Arp2/3 inhibitor, we found that the Arp2/3 complex and its activator, WASP, colocalized with the actin teeth (Figure 5a and b).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 5a and b.

claim: Cortactin and cofilin, actin-binding proteins that are frequently found in association with densely branched actin networks, also localized to the phagocytic teeth.
source: Moreover, cortactin and cofilin, actin-binding proteins that are frequently found in association with densely branched actin networks, also localized to the phagocytic teeth (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Myosin-II often appeared distinctly behind the actin teeth in an anti-correlated fashion.
source: In contrast, myosin-II often appeared distinctly behind the actin teeth in an anti-correlated fashion (Figure 5b).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Rings composed of myosin-II filaments could be seen within the phagocytic cup.
source: In particular, rings composed of myosin-II filaments could be seen within the phagocytic cup (Figure 5a).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: In cups that were almost closed, myosin-II coalesced into a ring behind the actin rim.
source: In cups that were almost closed, myosin-II coalesced into a ring behind the actin rim (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and clearly localized to sites of target constriction in cases of extreme target deformation (Figure 5c).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5c.

claim: The two long-tailed myosin-I isoforms, myo1e and myo1f, localized specifically to the tips of the actin teeth.
source: Meanwhile, the two long-tailed myosin-I isoforms, myo1e and myo1f, localized specifically to the tips of the actin teeth, consistent with our previous observations (Figure 5a; Barger et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 5a and comparison to cited previous work.

claim: Both paxillin and vinculin localized behind the phagocytic teeth in a punctate-like pattern.
source: In comparison to the branched actin-binding proteins, both paxillin and vinculin localized behind the phagocytic teeth in a punctate-like pattern (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Actin teeth are composed of branched actin filaments guided by myosin-I motor proteins.
source: Altogether, these studies support a model whereby actin teeth are composed of branched actin filaments guided by myosin-I motor proteins.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the localization of Arp2/3, WASP, and myosin-I to the teeth.

claim: The localization of myosin-II and paxillin/vinculin behind the teeth suggests that these proteins may play a role in the potential interconnection of the teeth, similar to podosomes on 2D surfaces.
source: The localization of myosin-II and paxillin/vinculin behind the teeth suggests that these proteins may play a role in the potential interconnection of the teeth, similar to podosomes on 2D surfaces (Meddens et al., 2016; van den Dries et al., 2019b).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the spatial localization patterns and comparison to cited literature on podosomes.

claim: Attempted partial eating attempts occurred in approximately 14% of all recorded phagocytic events.
source: Importantly, these encounters were rather common, with the attempted partial eating attempts (~14%) and popping (~24%) making up almost 40% off all recorded events (Figure 6e).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of phagocytic outcomes shown in Figure 6e.

claim: Popping events occurred in approximately 24% of all recorded phagocytic events.
source: Importantly, these encounters were rather common, with the attempted partial eating attempts (~14%) and popping (~24%) making up almost 40% off all recorded events (Figure 6e).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of phagocytic outcomes shown in Figure 6e.

claim: Popping events occurred much less frequently for stiffer 6.5 kPa targets (~1%, n = 89, p = 1.5 × 10–6).
source: Furthermore, such events, and specifically popping, were mechanosensitive and occurred much less frequently for stiffer 6.5 kPa targets (~1%, n = 89, p = 1.5 × 10–6), resulting in the overall more frequent failure of phagocytosis for soft particles (Figure 6f).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analysis of popping frequency on different stiffness targets shown in Figure 6f.

claim: Popping events are mechanosensitive.
source: Furthermore, such events, and specifically popping, were mechanosensitive and occurred much less frequently for stiffer 6.5 kPa targets (~1%, n = 89, p = 1.5 × 10–6), resulting in the overall more frequent failure of phagocytosis for soft particles (Figure 6f).
evidence: The claim is supported by the observation that popping frequency depends on target stiffness.

claim: Failure of phagocytosis is more frequent for soft particles compared to stiffer particles.
source: Furthermore, such events, and specifically popping, were mechanosensitive and occurred much less frequently for stiffer 6.5 kPa targets (~1%, n = 89, p = 1.5 × 10–6), resulting in the overall more frequent failure of phagocytosis for soft particles (Figure 6f).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 6f.

claim: FcR-mediated phagocytosis occurs through a unique mechanism in which normal forces dominate over shear forces in the cell-target interaction.
source: By combining LLSM and MP-TFM, we report here a detailed analysis of the mechanical progression of phagocytosis and the contributions of several key molecular players. We have discovered that FcR-mediated phagocytosis occurs through a unique mechanism in which normal forces dominate over shear forces in the cell-target interaction.
evidence: The claim is supported by force measurements showing normal forces are ~7-fold higher than shear forces (Figure 2d).

claim: The phagocytic cup is not equivalent to the leading edge of a migrating cell, where shear forces typically predominate at the cell-substrate interface.
source: This is in contrast to the current view that the phagocytic cup is equivalent to the leading edge of a migrating cell, where shear forces typically predominate at the cell-substrate interface (Case and Waterman, 2015; Legant et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that normal forces dominate in phagocytosis, contrasting with cited literature on cell migration.

claim: The fast forward movement of actin teeth concomitant with phagocytic cup progression is in stark contrast to lamellipodial focal adhesion complexes, which are fixed relative to the substratum.
source: In addition, the fast forward movement of actin teeth, which underlie target constriction, concomitant with phagocytic cup progression across the target is in stark contrast to lamellipodial focal adhesion complexes, which are fixed relative to the substratum (Case and Waterman, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by tracking data showing teeth movement (Figure 4e) and comparison to cited literature on cell migration.

claim: Strong normal forces and target constriction are likely a general feature of phagocytosis.
source: The strong target constriction recently observed in complement-mediated phagocytosis by peritoneal macrophages in vitro (Walbaum et al., 2021) and in phosphatidylserine-mediated phagocytosis by epithelial cells in zebrafish embryos (Hoijman et al., 2021) suggests that strong normal forces and target constriction are likely a general feature of phagocytosis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations in this study and comparison to cited recent literature on other phagocytic modes.

claim: Normal forces are primarily generated by protrusive phagocytic actin 'teeth' and myosin-II contractility, which make distinct contributions to target constriction.
source: We show that these normal forces are primarily generated by protrusive phagocytic actin 'teeth' and myosin-II contractility, which make distinct contributions to target constriction.
evidence: The claim is supported by drug inhibition studies (Figure 3) and force analysis (Figure 2).

claim: The Arp2/3 complex was not required for FcR-mediated ingestion of smaller phagocytic targets, while the uptake of particles comparable in size to those in this study (~10 μm) was Arp2/3-dependent.
source: A previous study showed that the Arp2/3 complex was not required for FcR-mediated ingestion of smaller phagocytic targets, while the uptake of particles comparable in size to those in our study (~10 μm) was Arp2/3-dependent (Rotty et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature.

claim: Inhibition of the Arp2/3 complex dramatically reduces actin tooth number and size, and ultimately target constriction and uptake efficiency.
source: This is consistent with our observations that inhibition of the Arp2/3 complex dramatically reduces actin tooth number and size, and ultimately target constriction and uptake efficiency.
evidence: The claim is supported by drug inhibition studies shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Myosin-II inhibition in studies on podosomes caused a reduction in podosome stiffness and protrusive activity.
source: Inhibition of myosin-II in studies on podosomes also caused a reduction in podosome stiffness and protrusive activity (Labernadie et al., 2014; Labernadie et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature.

claim: In 2D podosomes, myosin-II filaments interconnect radial actin fibers of individual podosomes to create a coherent network.
source: In 2D podosomes, myosin-II filaments interconnect radial actin fibers of individual podosomes to create a coherent network (Labernadie et al., 2014; Meddens et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature.

claim: Actin teeth in phagocytosis may be comparably interconnected by actomyosin structures, bearing similarity to the organization of podosome rosettes.
source: The localization of myosin-II behind and in between teeth, as well as the coordinated movement of teeth at the mesoscale, suggests that actin teeth in phagocytosis may be comparably interconnected by actomyosin structures, bearing similarity to the organization of podosome rosettes (Linder, 2007).
evidence: The claim is inferred from localization data (Figure 5) and movement coordination (Figure 4e) with comparison to cited literature.

claim: Individual teeth grow larger and stronger with phagocytic progression, correlating with increasing myosin-II constriction observed in late-stage phagocytosis.
source: We find that individual teeth grow larger and stronger with phagocytic progression, correlating with increasing myosin-II constriction observed in late-stage phagocytosis (Figure 7a).
evidence: The claim is supported by stage-specific analysis shown in Figure 4h and force analysis in Figure 3.

claim: Mechanical resistance makes self-assembling actin networks stronger through a force feedback mechanism.
source: These observations may relate to the force feedback mechanism observed in Arp2/3-mediated branched actin networks in vitro showing that mechanical resistance makes self-assembling actin networks stronger (Bieling et al., 2016; Li et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature.

claim: Increased myosin-II contraction in late-stage phagocytosis may promote stronger actin teeth.
source: Thus, increased myosin-II contraction in late-stage phagocytosis may promote stronger actin teeth.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between myosin-II activity and tooth properties with reference to force feedback mechanisms.

claim: Rapid structural reinforcement by myosin-II has not yet been described for actin cores of podosomes on 2D, and may be unique to phagocytosis.
source: This rapid structural reinforcement by myosin-II has not yet been described for actin cores of podosomes on 2D, and may be unique to phagocytosis.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison to existing literature on podosomes and speculation about phagocytosis-specific mechanisms.

claim: Myosin-II plays an important role in phagocytic cup closure.
source: We further show that myosin-II plays an important role in phagocytic cup closure – a stage in phagocytosis that has been notoriously difficult to study experimentally (Marie-Anaïs et al., 2016; Figure 7a).
evidence: The claim is supported by the accumulation of late-stage cups upon Blebbistatin treatment (Figure 3h).

claim: Myosin-II is generally not deemed important for cup closure or phagocytic progression.
source: Generally, myosin-II is not deemed important for cup closure or phagocytic progression (Jaumouillé and Waterman, 2020; Swanson et al., 1999), yet we observe myosin-II enrichment at the rim of phagocytic cups (Figure 5c).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature.

claim: Blebbistatin treatment specifically affects late-stage contractile force generation causing cup closure to become a bottleneck step.
source: Moreover, Blebbistatin treatment specifically affects late-stage contractile force generation (Figure 3h) causing cup closure to become a bottleneck step as evidenced by the accumulation of late-stage phagocytic cups (Figure 3g).
evidence: The claim is supported by stage-specific analysis of drug effects shown in Figure 3g and 3h.

claim: The contribution of myosin-II activity to phagocytic progression has likely gone unnoticed in previous studies using the most common implementation of TFM on a planar substrate, which only measures forces that are tangential to the surface (shear).
source: Because these forces are exerted normal to the target surface, the contribution of myosin-II activity to phagocytic progression has likely gone unnoticed in previous studies using the most common implementation of TFM on a planar substrate, which only measures forces that are tangential to the surface (shear) (Barger et al., 2019; Jaumouillé et al., 2019; Kovari et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that myosin-II generates normal forces and comparison to cited literature using planar TFM.

claim: FcR-mediated phagocytosis is hallmarked by a unique force balance, where before 50% engulfment, target constriction results in an outward force balanced by pulling forces throughout the base of the phagocytic cup.
source: We show that FcR-mediated phagocytosis is hallmarked by a unique force balance, where before 50% engulfment, target constriction results in an outward force balanced by pulling forces throughout the base of the phagocytic cup (Figure 7b).
evidence: The claim is supported by force analysis shown in Figure 2j and Figure 7b.

claim: The pulling forces at the base of the cup are most likely not due to actin polymerization forces or actomyosin contractility, but instead a result of the target being held in place through receptor-ligand bonds.
source: Given the reduced presence of cytoskeletal components at the base of the cup (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Freeman and Grinstein, 2014; Jaumouillé and Waterman, 2020), these pulling forces are most likely not due to actin polymerization forces or actomyosin contractility, but instead a result of the target being held in place through receptor-ligand bonds throughout the base of the cup.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of pulling forces at the cup base where cytoskeletal components are sparse.

claim: The forces acting on receptor-ligand bonds within the cup are likely dependent on the target physical properties and the local geometry at the rim of the cup.
source: Hence, the forces acting on receptor-ligand bonds within the cup are likely dependent on the target physical properties and the local geometry at the rim of the cup (Figure 7b).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the force balance analysis and geometric considerations shown in Figure 7b.

claim: The push-and-lock mechanism may enable sensing of physical target properties through a proofreading mechanism and thereby aid macrophages in target selection.
source: Since the lifetime of such bonds is tension-dependent (Nishi et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2019), this push-and-lock mechanism may enable sensing of physical target properties through a proofreading mechanism and thereby aid macrophages in target selection.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the force balance and cited literature on tension-dependent bond lifetimes.

claim: For non-spherical targets (e.g. ellipsoidal), the force balance would result in a net torque aligning the target's long axis along the phagocytic axis, which has been observed previously and is reported to lead to enhanced uptake efficiency of ellipsoidal targets.
source: In addition, for non-spherical targets (e.g. ellipsoidal), this force balance would result in a net torque aligning the target's long axis along the phagocytic axis, which has been observed previously and is reported to lead to enhanced uptake efficiency of ellipsoidal targets (Champion and Mitragotri, 2006; Schuerle et al., 2017; Sosale et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the force balance analysis and comparison to cited literature on ellipsoidal target uptake.

claim: Target constriction could be important for creating a tight apposition between the cell and target, which is essential for receptor engagement.
source: Aside from a role in cup closure, target constriction could be important for creating a tight apposition between the cell and target, which is essential for receptor engagement (Bakalar et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the observed constriction and cited literature on receptor engagement.

claim: Overly strong target constriction leads to failure of attempted phagocytosis, expressed either as partial eating or a popping mechanism leading to forfeit of uptake.
source: Surprisingly though, we noticed that overly strong target constriction leads to failure of attempted phagocytosis, expressed either as partial eating or a popping mechanism leading in forfeit of uptake.
evidence: The claim is supported by observations of failed phagocytosis events shown in Figure 6.

claim: Partial eating and popping mechanisms may lead to reduced uptake efficiency in isolated phagocyte-target interaction, but may be critical in more complex phagocytic encounters that occur in vivo.
source: Although these mechanisms may lead to reduced uptake efficiency in isolated phagocyte-target interaction, we suspect they may be critical in more complex phagocytic encounters that occur in vivo, for example, when multiple macrophages approach a single target (Figure 6g), or attempt to engulf adherent and hard-to-reach targets (Colucci-Guyon et al., 2011; Davidson and Wood, 2020; Vorselen et al., 2020a).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on observations of complex encounters and cited literature.

claim: Actin polymerization-dependent protrusive forces and myosin-II-dependent contractile forces contribute to target deformation and phagocytic internalization.
source: Altogether, our findings show that actin polymerization-dependent protrusive forces and myosin-II-dependent contractile forces contribute to target deformation and phagocytic internalization, and likely both participate in the mechanosensation required for phagocytic plasticity.
evidence: The claim is supported by drug inhibition studies and force analysis throughout the manuscript.

claim: Actin polymerization-dependent protrusive forces and myosin-II-dependent contractile forces likely both participate in the mechanosensation required for phagocytic plasticity.
source: Altogether, our findings show that actin polymerization-dependent protrusive forces and myosin-II-dependent contractile forces contribute to target deformation and phagocytic internalization, and likely both participate in the mechanosensation required for phagocytic plasticity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the mechanosensitive behaviors observed (tooth formation, popping) and the roles of different molecular players.
